content:
A systematic review of 50 naturalistic classroom studies identified learner responses to WCF and stakeholder beliefs as major themes (Mao et al., 2024). Most included studies were qualitative (66.0%) and only 22.0% were theoretically motivated (Mao et al., 2024).

In a peer-mediated revision study, paper ratings improved by a mean of 1.1 points out of 7 between drafts (t(11) = 6.51, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 1.62), which the authors interpret as meaningful improvement following feedback-driven revision (Li & Hebert, 2023). Notably, participants acted on both higher-order content and low-level language issues, contrary to earlier findings that students make only low-level revisions on second drafts (Li & Hebert, 2023). The authors state that a causal role for students' self-reflections was not established (Li & Hebert, 2023).

Four students ignored unity-related peer feedback and two ignored word-use-related feedback (Li & Hebert, 2023), while in an ethnographic case study of a doctoral writing group, 93 of 99 segmented peer comments were rated useful or very useful (Yallop et al., 2021). The latter study's small, single-group design limits generalizability, and the authors make no claim of reproducibility (Yallop et al., 2021). Affect was not coded because evidence was insufficient for reliable coding (Yallop et al., 2021).

In a 16-week case study, teacher feedback addressed more error types (16) than automated feedback (8), though assignment differences may have influenced this (Zhang & Hyland, 2018). The same study found that the highly engaged learner outperformed the moderately engaged learner in responding to both feedback sources (Zhang & Hyland, 2018).

sentences: Research on written corrective feedback (WCF) in second-language (L2) writing has moved from asking whether feedback works to asking how learners engage with it and how teacher, peer, and automated sources compare.

This review synthesizes the project library on peer-provided WCF, organized around three themes: effects on accuracy and revision, engagement and uptake, and the comparative positioning of peer feedback against teacher and automated feedback.
Evidence on accuracy gains from peer feedback is limited and largely indirect.

In a peer-mediated revision study, paper ratings improved by a mean of 1.1 points out of 7 between drafts (t(11) = 6.51, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 1.62), which the authors interpret as meaningful improvement following feedback-driven revision (Li & Hebert, 2023).

A strength of this design is the objective rubric-based scoring; a limitation is that the design cannot attribute gains to peer feedback specifically, and the authors state that a causal role for students' self-reflections was not established (Li & Hebert, 2023).
Notably, participants acted on both higher-order content and low-level language issues, contrary to earlier findings that students make only low-level revisions on second drafts (Li & Hebert, 2023).
for direct comparisons of accuracy gains under peer versus teacher feedback.
Uptake is uneven.

Four students ignored unity-related peer feedback and two ignored word-use-related feedback (Li & Hebert, 2023), while in an ethnographic case study of a doctoral writing group, 93 of 99 segmented peer comments were rated useful or very useful (Yallop et al., 2021).
The latter study's small, single-group design limits generalizability, and the authors make no claim of reproducibility (Yallop et al., 2021).
A further limitation is that affect was not coded because evidence was insufficient for reliable coding (Yallop et al., 2021), leaving the emotional dimension of peer feedback unexamined.
on how peer feedback compares with teacher or automated feedback in promoting revision behaviour.
Comparative evidence is sparse.
In a 16-week case study, teacher feedback addressed more error types (16) than automated feedback (8), though assignment differences may have influenced this (Zhang & Hyland, 2018).
The same study found that the highly engaged learner outperformed the moderately engaged learner in responding to both feedback sources (Zhang & Hyland, 2018).

A systematic review of 50 naturalistic classroom studies identified learner responses to WCF and stakeholder beliefs as major themes (Mao et al., 2024), but most included studies were qualitative (66.0%) and only 22.0% were theoretically motivated (Mao et al., 2024), constraining causal inference.
Peer WCF is associated with revision improvements and generally positive usefulness ratings, yet evidence is dominated by small, qualitative, single-context designs.
Three gaps follow: no direct experimental comparison of peer, teacher, and automated WCF on accuracy; limited evidence on uptake conditions; and an unexamined affective dimension.
These gaps motivate the present study's comparative design.

quotes: A systematic search generated 50 empirical studies that met our inclusion criteria for the current review, which revealed four major themes: (1) teacher WCF practices in L2 writing classrooms, (2) L2 learner responses to WCF, (3) stakeholders’ beliefs and perspectives on WCF, and (4) WCF-related motivation and emotions.
A systematic review was conducted by the review team to synthesize and interpret findings accumulated across individual primary studies.
there is not yet a synthesis of naturalistic classroom studies where the type and amount of feedback provided on students’ writing performance is not manipulated or controlled

uncited_sentences.sentence: Research on written corrective feedback (WCF) in second-language (L2) writing has shifted from asking whether feedback works to asking how learners engage with it and how teacher, peer, and automated sources compare [NEEDS CITATION].
Evidence on the accuracy effects of peer feedback is limited and largely indirect [NEEDS CITATION].
Uptake of peer comments is uneven.
Comparative evidence on teacher versus automated feedback is sparse.

Across these sources, peer WCF is associated with revision improvements and generally positive usefulness ratings, yet the evidence base is dominated by small, qualitative, single-context designs [NEEDS CITATION].

Three gaps follow: no direct experimental comparison of peer, teacher, and automated WCF on accuracy; limited evidence on the conditions governing uptake; and an affective dimension that remains unexamined [NEEDS CITATION].
